kernelIdea: A set is a well-defined collection; x ∈ S says x belongs. Sets are unordered and repetition is irrelevant. The empty set is a set. ℕ, ℤ, ℝ are the standard number sets.

kernels.l1: A box needs a rule everyone agrees on. Then you always know what is in and what is out.
kernels.l2: A box of things needs a rule that everybody agrees on. The order does not matter, saying a thing twice does not matter, and an empty box is still a box.
kernels.l3: A set is a collection with a rule clear enough that everyone agrees what is in it. We write x ∈ S for "x is in S". Order and repeats do not change a set, and the empty set { } is a set.
kernels.l4: A set is a well-defined collection of objects; x ∈ S asserts membership and x ∉ S denies it. Sets are unordered and repetition-insensitive, ∅ is a set, and ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℝ are the standard number sets.
kernels.l5: A set is determined entirely by which objects belong to it: {a,b} = {b,a} = {a,a,b}. Well-definedness means membership is unambiguous for every candidate object.
kernels.l6: Sets are extensional objects: two sets are equal exactly when they have the same members, so order and multiplicity are invisible. "Set" is deliberately left undefined in naive set theory.
kernels.l7: A set is a well-defined collection, determined by its members alone; x ∈ S is the primitive relation, ∅ is a set, and the number systems ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ are the standard examples.
kernels.l8: Set is an undefined primitive constrained by axioms; extensionality makes membership the whole content of a set, and the well-definedness requirement is what Russell's paradox forces us to take seriously.
